content_list.content_text: In the 1990s, European cinema tried to establish a continental identity in the face of what was perceived as Hollywood's cultural imperialism. In the newly redrawn countries of Eastern and Central Europe, filmmakers sought a balance between the desire for a distinctive national cinema and recognition as part of the European tradition. Partly as a consequence of the Cold War, these countries had long-established domestic markets for popular productions, and it fell to just a few directors to make the films with the broadest appeal.

information.contentText: Starring Vincent Cassel, Hubert Koundé and Saïd Taghmaoui, the film follows 24 hours in the lives of three friends who live in a poor, immigrant neighborhood of Paris and set off on a night-time journey during which they are caught by the police.

content_list.content_text: In Hungary, Béla Tarr's (b. 1955) epic Sátántangó (Satantango, 1994) confirmed the director as a natural successor to Miklós Jancsó (b. 1921) and István Szabó (b. 1938). In the former Yugoslavia, Emir Kusturica (b. 1954) dethroned Dušan Makavejev (1932-2019) with films such as Underground (1995) - a surreal comedy about Yugoslavia since World War II. Both Tarr and Kusturica won international acclaim, which brought few benefits to the filmmakers of their countries.

In Poland, Andrzej Wajda (b. 1926) had handed the role of great national filmmaker to Krzysztof Kieślowski (1941-1996) in the 1980s, but the national-icon status of both was undermined by the fact that they moved to France, for political reasons and also drawn by better financial conditions. This behavior was far from rare: Kieślowski's "Three Colors trilogy" (1993-1994), named after the colors of the French flag, was produced by the Romanian-born Marin Karmitz (b. 1938), the same producer who later lured Michael Haneke (b. 1942) from Austria to France.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from All About My Mother
information.contentText: Almodóvar dedicates his film "To all actresses who have played actresses. To all women who act. To men who act and become women. To all the people who want to be mothers. To my mother."

content_list.content_text: Collaborations of this kind not only raise questions about a film's nationality - the "Three Colors" trilogy is made up of French-Polish productions, two of them in French and one largely in Polish - but also suggest that Europe works as a microcosm of the international film industry at a time when Western Europe is losing its rising talent to Hollywood, just as Eastern Europe is losing its own to France.

quote.quote: Director Michael Haneke sets out to deconstruct and critique practically all of the cinema that came before – confronting the audience with its own hypocrisy.
quote.author: Kim Newman on Funny Games

content_list.content_text: French film production in this period was paved by a series of expensive, large-scale productions inspired by French literary and historical traditions, usually starring big names. The success of Cyrano de Bergerac (1990), by Jean-Paul Rappeneau (b. 1932), along with that of Jean de Florette (1986), by Claude Berri (1934-2009), turned Gérard Depardieu into an internationally renowned star.

information.contentText: The film frequently blurs the line between fiction and reality, placing particular emphasis on the act of watching. The character Paul breaks the fourth wall throughout the film and addresses the camera in various ways. As he guides Anna in the search for her dead dog, he turns, winks and smiles at the camera.

content_list.content_text: At the same time, a series of low-budget films by younger directors used Hollywood techniques to express a singular aesthetic vision. The decade saw the rise of major talents such as Jean-Pierre Jeunet (b. 1953) and Marc Caro (b. 1956), who burst onto the international scene with Delicatessen (1991), a surreal black comedy set in a post-apocalyptic France. The highly stylized portrayal of suburban youth by Mathieu Kassovitz (b. 1967) in La Haine (Hate, 1995) focuses on themes of social integration that were on the agenda in contemporary France and resonated internationally. Like Luc Besson (b. 1959), both Jeunet and Kassovitz went on to make films in the United States.

Hollywood's siren song had a damaging impact on Germany, as many of the talents of the previous decade - Wolfgang Petersen (b. 1941) and Roland Emmerich (b. 1955) - also jumped ship. What's more, the promise and prestige attached to the New German Cinema of the 1970s had sunk.

information.contentText: The film contains two allusions to Alfred Hitchcock's Vertigo. As in Hitchcock's film, it features recurring images of spirals, such as the Spirale bar behind Manni's phone booth and the spiral staircase Lola runs down. In addition, the painting on the back wall of the casino, showing a woman's head seen from behind, is based on a still from Vertigo.

content_list.content_text: German cinema struggled to express an identity of its own, and no filmmakers with a consistent body of work emerged. Toward the end of the decade, the romantic thrillers of Tom Tykwer (b. 1965), Winterschläfer (Winter Sleepers, 1997) and Lola rennt (Run Lola Run, 1998), offered inspiring hope for the future, but soon afterward he too followed the well-worn path that leads to Hollywood.

In southern Europe, the Italian film industry looked back on the past with nostalgia. Drawing on Neorealism and the comedies of Totò to repeat the success of Nuovo Cinema Paradiso (Cinema Paradiso, 1988), directed by Giuseppe Tornatore (b. 1956), came Il postino (The Postman, 1994), starring French star Philippe Noiret and directed by Englishman Michael Radford (b. 1946), and La vita è bella (Life Is Beautiful, 1997), by Roberto Benigni (b. 1952). Pedro Almodóvar (b. 1949) had dominated the national cinema for some time with his esoteric, eccentric vision of post-Franco Spain, filtered through the manic, color-saturated lenses of melodrama, comedy and surrealism. He continued to succeed with films such as La flor de mi secreto (The Flower of My Secret, 1995) and Todo sobre mi madre (All About My Mother, 1999). However, he had to share the laurels with Julio Medem (b. 1958), who debuted with the rural drama Vacas (Cows, 1992), and the Chilean Alejandro Amenábar (b. 1972), whose thriller Abre los ojos (Open Your Eyes, 1997) drew enough international attention to earn a Hollywood remake under the title Vanilla Sky (2001), with Penélope Cruz again in the lead role.

information.contentTitle: Trailer for Dancer in the Dark
information.contentText: Dancer in the Dark completes von Trier's "Golden Heart" trilogy, which includes Breaking the Waves and Idioterne. The film's soundtrack, released on the album Selmasongs, was created entirely by its lead actress and musician Björk.

content_list.content_text: It fell to two Danish directors, Lars von Trier (b. 1956) and Thomas Vinterberg (b. 1969), to make the seminal attempt at a rebirth of national cinema in this period, with a European outlook. At a symposium held in Paris in 1995 to celebrate cinema's first century, they presented the Dogme 95 Manifesto and a "Vow of Chastity," a set of rules intended to free artists from the need to compete with Hollywood. Presenting itself as a "rescue action" against the excesses of big-budget filmmaking, the Dogme 95 movement set out to counter "certain tendencies" in cinema - a deliberate reference to the famous article "Une certaine tendance du cinéma français" (A Certain Tendency of French Cinema) by François Truffaut (1932-1984), published in the magazine Cahiers du cinéma in 1954. It vowed to overturn modern cinema's cosmetic preoccupations, the predictability of its plots and the superficiality of its action.

content_list.title: Dogma 95 and the Essence of Cinema
content_list.description:
The Dogma 95 movement was an initiative of Danish filmmakers Lars von Trier and Thomas Vinterberg and is regarded as one of the greatest initiatives in film history. It grew out of its official document, called The Manifesto, published on March 13, 1995, in the Danish city of Copenhagen and presented to the whole community at an international symposium on the centenary of cinema. The movement's main proposal was to create a more realistic, less commercial cinema that, in its creators' view, would recover the essence of cinema.

The Manifesto signed by Lars von Trier and Thomas Vinterberg focused on criticizing the overproduction of films, as well as the habit of treating them as true works of art. The idea of treating cinema like a painter's canvas, as well as the use of a range of devices that gave films an exaggeratedly artificial tone, was firmly rejected by both directors. The argument that audiences should not be deceived and that technology took away the director's power as the author of his own work also appears among the Manifesto's ideas. The document also included the "Vow of Chastity," which set out ten principles to be followed under the Dogma 95 movement. They are:

Shooting must be done on location. Props and sets must not be brought in (if a particular prop is necessary for the story, a location must be chosen where this prop is to be found).
The sound must never be produced apart from the images or vice versa. (Music must therefore not be used.)
The camera must be handheld. Any movement - or immobility - attainable by hand is permitted. (The film must not take place where the camera is standing; shooting must take place where the film takes place.)
The film must be in color. Special lighting is not acceptable. (If there is too much light, the scene must be cut, or a single lamp may be attached to the camera.) Optical work and filters are forbidden.
The film must not contain any "superficial" action. (Murders, weapons and the like must never occur.)
Temporal and geographical alienation are forbidden. (That is to say, the film takes place in real time.)
Genre films are not acceptable.
The film format must be standard 35 mm.
The director must not be credited.

In 2005, new principles were added to the Manifesto, to apply to films released from the following year onward. They are:

Filming must be done in digital format.
Shooting must take place in Scotland;
Shooting cannot exceed a period of 6 weeks;
The total cost of the film cannot exceed one million pounds sterling.

Despite being innovative, the Manifesto is also seen as controversial. Its ideas and films diverge on some points, and the rules are almost impossible to follow. The document's own authors did not follow them strictly. A classic example is Dogville (2003), directed by von Trier, which, although it followed many of the document's rules, was not recognized by Dogma 95.

By proposing the most faithful possible representation of reality, the Manifesto's creators overlook the fact that reality is not objective. A film's director, like any other human being, has a personal view of things - in other words, is not impartial. This is reflected in how the film is made, what preferences it will have, how the camera is positioned in a scene and how the dialogue will convey what one wants to say. Thus, the representation will never be entirely what is real. Another contradiction is not crediting the director when he will be stamping his own vision on the work.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the article "Dogma 95 e a essência do cinema" (Dogma 95 and the Essence of Cinema), by Fernando Pivetti and Luiza Fernandes, in Jornalismo Junior.

content_list.content_text: The first Dogme film was Festen (The Celebration, 1998), shot on Sony Hi-8 video, which follows the story of a family torn apart by a suicide. Von Trier's first venture within the Dogme precepts was Idioterne (The Idiots, 1998), which became notorious for its frank treatment of sexuality and disability. The success of The Celebration, together with the notoriety of The Idiots, earned Dogme a global audience. By 1999, the movement had already spread to France with Lovers (1999), by Jean-Marc Barr (b. 1960), and to the United States with Julien Donkey-Boy (1999), by Harmony Korine (b. 1973). It became a worldwide phenomenon and, ironically, by looking into the very guts of Europe, Dogme 95 gave birth to a movement with global impact.

quote.quote: Run Lola Run could easily be the most succinct piece of conceptual art ever released in cinemas, a shock dose of German existentialist cinema.
quote.author: Ed Gonzalez on Run Lola Run

content_list.content_text: Some smaller countries whose output seemed likewise to center on one or two directors - such as Greece with Theodoros Angelopoulos (b. 1935), Portugal with Pedro Costa (b. 1959) and Manoel de Oliveira (1908-2015), or Austria with Haneke - struggled to have their remarkable films labeled "European" rather than hailed as signs of a supposed new wave. Angelopoulos's Mia Aioniotita Kai Mia Mera (Eternity and a Day, 1998) follows a cinematic tradition of depicting the universal theme of a dying man making peace with life. Yet throughout the decade, the tendency to identify individual films as national rather than European seemed almost impossible to change.

information.contentText: To avoid breaking one of the Dogme 95 rules, which forbids the use of non-diegetic music, a harmonica player was recorded during the shooting of some scenes, including the end credits, even though he is never seen on screen.

content_list.content_text: Thus Haneke, German by birth and raised in Austria, struggled throughout the decade to shake off the common view of his films as indictments of Austrian society rather than of Western culture as a whole - even when, as happened with his parody of the thriller, Funny Games (1997), he shot in an unspecified location that could have been anywhere in rural Europe, with language as the only clue to the film's origin. Or Von Trier, regarded as essentially a Danish director, yet whose films rarely refer to Denmark. It is only when directors leave their countries that they manage to escape national borders: a testament to the complexity of the tension between nation and Europe that defines the decade.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Catherine Wheatley, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

movies.overview: Two psychotic young men take a mother, father, and son hostage in their vacation cabin and force them to play sadistic "games" with one another for their own amusement.
movies.title: Funny Games

movies.overview: After a chaotic night of rioting in a marginal suburb of Paris, three young friends, Vinz, Hubert and Saïd, wander around unoccupied waiting for news about the state of health of a mutual friend who has been seriously injured when confronting the police.
movies.title: La Haine

movies.overview: A single mother in Madrid sees her only son die on his birthday as he runs to seek an actress' autograph. Beside herself with grief, she returns to Barcelona to tell the boy's father about the death of the son he never knew he had.
movies.title: All About My Mother

movies.overview: Lola receives a phone call from her boyfriend Manni. He lost 100,000 DM in a subway train that belongs to a very bad guy. She has 20 minutes to raise this amount and meet Manni. Otherwise, he will rob a store to get the money. Three different alternatives may happen depending on some minor event along Lola's run.
movies.title: Run Lola Run

movies.overview: A very handsome man finds the love of his life, but he suffers an accident and needs to have his face rebuilt by surgery after it is severely disfigured.
movies.title: Open Your Eyes

movies.overview: Selma, a Czech immigrant on the verge of blindness, struggles to make ends meet for herself and her son, who has inherited the same genetic disorder and will suffer the same fate without an expensive operation. When life gets too difficult, Selma learns to cope through her love of musicals, escaping life's troubles - even if just for a moment - by dreaming up little numbers to the rhythmic beats of her surroundings.
movies.title: Dancer in the Dark

movies.overview: A grandiose party to celebrate a sixtieth birthday unleashes a family drama with all the lies that conceal horrendous secrets. The eldest son, Christian, stages a showdown with the popular pater familias; his provocative, moving after-dinner speech dislodges all the masks, which finally fall completely as the father-son conflict intensifies and the bewildered guests look on.
movies.title: The Celebration

movies.overview: With his first Dogma-95 film director Lars von Trier opens up a completely new film platform. With a mix of home-video and documentary styles the film tells the story of a group of young people who have decided to get to know their “inner-idiots” and thus not only facing and breaking their outer appearance but also their inner.
movies.title: The Idiots

movies.overview: A touching story of an Italian book seller of Jewish ancestry who lives in his own little fairy tale. His creative and happy life would come to an abrupt halt when his entire family is deported to a concentration camp during World War II. While locked up he tries to convince his son that the whole thing is just a game.
movies.title: Life Is Beautiful

movies.overview: Simple Italian postman learns to love poetry while delivering mail to a famous poet; he uses this to woo local beauty Beatrice.
movies.title: The Postman

movies.overview: A filmmaker recalls his childhood, when he fell in love with the movies at his village's theater and formed a deep friendship with the theater's projectionist.
movies.title: Cinema Paradiso
